Modulation of T Cell Trafficking to the Small and Large Intestine Mucosa

Abstract

Infections of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract have a high disease burden globally, and

effective vaccines are needed to reduce the spread of many GI pathogens. A majority of clinical

and pre-clinical vaccines are delivered parenterally, such as by subcutaneous (s.c.) or intramuscular

(i.m.) injections. While these routes are effective at establishing systemic protection, they are often

poor at eliciting protective antibodies and T cell responses in the gut, leaving the mucosa

susceptible to pathogen entry, and possibly replication and transmission.

Therefore, a strategy that generates gut-tropic T cells in a parenteral immunization has the

potential to improve vaccine efficacy, which is presented in my dissertation. Modulation of CD8+

T cell trafficking was achieved by adjuvantation with “gut-imprinting” signals – tissue-specific

cues that promote entry (“homing”) of antigen-experienced lymphocytes into the gut, through up-

regulation of homing molecules.

I immunized mice s.c. with a model antigen chicken ovalbumin (OVA) and an adjuvant

CpG, in combination with gut-imprinting compounds. Vaccine supplementation with all-trans

retinoic acid (ATRA) as well as Am80, a synthetic retinoic acid receptor (RAR) agonist, increased

expression of small intestine homing molecules α4β7 and CCR9, increased T cell trafficking to the

small intestine, and established resident-memory T (Trm) cells. Additionally, an Am80-

encapsulating polymeric nanoparticle was developed which showed equivalent gut-imprinting

capacity and improved clinical translatability, compared to the un-encapsulated Am80.


<!-- Page 7 -->


iv

Unlike the small intestine, Am80 alone was sub-optimal at targeting CD8+ T cells to the

large intestine. Optimal targeting to the cecum and colon required a combination of RAR agonist

(Am80) and aryl-hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) agonist (10-CL-BBQ), respectively up-regulating

α4β7 and the large intestine homing molecule GPR15. Both the RAR-α4β7 axis and AHR-GPR15

axis were indispensable for large intestine trafficking, whereas AHR was dispensable for small

intestine trafficking, suggesting a mechanism for compartmentalized T cell entry into different

segments of the GI tract. In the s.c. vaccination model, combined administration of Am80 and 10-

CL-BBQ yielded the most robust large intestine trafficking α4β7+GPR15+ effector T (Teff) cells,

established Trm cells in the total intestinal tract, and conferred protection against intra-rectal

challenge with Listeria Monocytogenes.

In summary, I conclude that CD8+ T cell trafficking to the small and large intestine are

differentially regulated by the RAR and AHR signaling pathways, and that adjuvantation of

parenteral vaccines with agonists of RAR and AHR are viable approaches to enhance T cell

protection of the intestinal tract.

### 1.1 DISSERTATION OVERVIEW

The intestinal immune system is involved in many physiological and pathological contexts.

Particularly, CD8+ T cells in the gut mucosal barrier play important roles in defense against

infections, as well as in other diseases such as intestinal cancers. My dissertation is aimed at

understanding the mechanisms of CD8+ T cell trafficking to the small and large intestine, and at

utilizing this process to improve vaccine responses in the intestinal tract.

Chapter One gives an introduction to intestinal immunity and T cell gut-trafficking and

reviews literature on the topic. Chapter Two is focused on targeting the retinoic acid receptor

(RAR) to promote small intestine T cell trafficking, and reports on a novel nano-carrier formulation

to deliver RAR agonists. Chapter Three is focused on mechanisms of CD8+ T cell trafficking to

the large intestine, highlighting the requirements for both RAR and aryl-hydrocarbon receptor

(AHR) signaling. Chapter Four provides a summary and discussion of my work.

This dissertation contains collaborative work with many colleagues. Specifically, I would

like to acknowledge Bruno Raposo, Ph.D., who pioneered the gut-trafficking project in the lab,

and Flora Tierney, our former lab technician who worked closely with me. Other specific

acknowledgements are given at respective sections and experiments.

### 1.2 THE INTESTINAL IMMUNE SYSTEM

### 1.2.1 The Gastrointestinal Tract

The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is a key part of the digestive system and serves important

functions in food intake and nutrient absorption. It is made up of multiple organs with a continuous

mucosal lining, specifically the mouth, throat, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large

intestine.


<!-- Page 13 -->


3

The intestinal tract, which consists of the small intestine and large intestine, is the major

location where many dietary compounds are absorbed and metabolized. The small intestine is

further divided into the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum (Treuting et al., 2017b). The large intestine

is further divided into cecum, colon (ascending, transverse and descending), rectum and anus

(Treuting et al., 2017a).

With a large epithelial surface area, measured around 1.42m2 in mice (Casteleyn et al.,

2010), the intestines are a complex interface between the body and outside environment. Besides

digesting food, the gut also serves important immune functions as a barrier tissue, defending the

body against pathogen invasions. Additionally, the intestines, particularly the large intestine,

harbor a vast community of microbes (gut microbiota). The crosstalk of metabolites, nutrients and

secreted factors play an important role in shaping intestinal physiology and pathology.

### 1.2.2 Structure and Cells of the Intestinal Immune System

The intestinal organ consists of four layers, the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria

and serosa. The mucosa is the layer closest to the lumen and consists of mucus, the single-cell

epithelial layer, the lamina propria and the muscularis mucosae.

The intestinal mucosa is interspersed with gut-associated lymphoid tissues (GALT). The

small intestine is interspersed with Peyer’s Patches, while the large intestine contains caecal patch

(Clark et al., 1994), colonic patches, and isolated lymphoid aggregates that may form depending

on immune challenge (Baptista et al., 2013).

The small intestine and colon drain into distinct lymph nodes in the mesenteric lymph node

(mLN) chain, and the colon also drains to separate lymph nodes outside of the mLNs (Houston et

al., 2016a). Along with this anatomical segmentation, it has also been proposed that the draining


<!-- Page 14 -->


4

LNs for small intestine and colon have different environments, leading to different immune

phenotypes in T cells activated in small intestine and colon draining LNs (Esterházy et al., 2019a;

Veenbergen et al., 2017a).

The small and large intestine are classified to have Type I mucosa, lined with a single layer

of columnar epithelium. Various types of immune cells populate the epithelium and lamina propria,

including T cells, plasma cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, innate lymphoid cells, etc. (Figure

1.1). These cells, together with secreted mediators of host defense (mucus, anti-microbial peptides,

etc.), orchestrate immune responses in health and disease.

### 1.3 VACCINATION AGAINST ENTERIC PATHOGENS

### 1.3.1 Infections and Diseases of the Intestinal Tract

The intestinal tract comes into close contact with the external environment, including food,

pathogens, and the gut microbiota. It is pivotal for the intestinal immune system to effectively

defend against infections, while maintaining tolerance to innocuous antigens, such as dietary

compounds and symbiont metabolites.

Enteric infections by rotavirus, ETEC, shigella and other pathogens are the major cause of

diarrhea, which is the third leading cause of death in children 1-59 months of age. Globally, nearly

1.7 billion cases of childhood diarrhea occur every year, leading to around 443832 deaths in

children under the age of 5, and an additional 50851 deaths in children aged 5 to 9 years (World

Health Organization, 2024). Additionally, the colorectal mucosa is susceptible to cancers and

sexually transmitted pathogens. In many such instances, effective prophylactic and treatment

vaccines are needed to reduce global disease burden.

Of recent interest, SARS-CoV-2, the virus causing the COVID-19 global pandemic, has

also been shown to infect the intestinal tract and cause GI tract symptoms (Xiao et al., 2020),

highlighting the importance of gut defense across a broad spectrum of pathogens, both current and

emerging.

On the other hand, food allergies, inflammatory and autoimmune disorders in the gut are

also increasingly prevalent (Gupta et al., 2019; Ng et al., 2017), particularly in industrialized

countries. Breaking of oral immune tolerance, often with the involvement of aberrant T cell

responses, is implicated in the pathogenesis of many such diseases, where immune-modulatory

treatment strategies could bring clinical benefits.

### 1.3.2 Vaccine Development against Intestinal Tract Infections

To-date, only a few vaccines against enteric illnesses are clinically approved (Table 1.1),

with an urgent unmet clinical need for vaccines against many more pathogens, such as ETEC,

Shigella and Norovirus (Eshaghi et al., 2024; GBD 2016 Diarrhoeal Disease Collaborators, 2018;

Lavelle & Ward, 2022; World Health Organization, n.d.).

*Table 1.1 Vaccines against GI tract Infections*


<!-- Page 17 -->


7

Additionally, a majority of the clinically approved vaccines are delivered orally, utilizing

inactivated and live attenuated pathogens. While this approach has the benefit of eliciting

protection in the GI tract mucosa, it also has several shortcomings: (1) live attenuated pathogens

may not be well-tolerated by people with compromised immune systems, and could cause adverse

effects as well as vaccine-derived outbreaks; (2) while many vaccines showed high efficacy in

developed countries, the efficacy decreases in developing countries where the pathogens are

endemic to, due to a stronger build-up of oral tolerance; (3) many novel vaccines platforms (mRNA

vaccines, DNA vaccines, protein subunit vaccines, etc) are difficult to administer orally, due to a

lack of effective mucosal adjuvants and the harsh GI tract environment (PH, protein degradation,

elimination by peristalsis, etc).

### 1.3.3 Parenteral Vaccination is Poor at Inducing Mucosal Responses

Vaccines administered parentally, on the other hand, can circumvent many challenges of

an oral vaccine. However, the protective efficacy against enteric infections is hampered by the lack

of local protection in the GI tract.

Defenses at the intestinal mucosa, by way of tissue-resident memory T cells (Trm) and

mucosal antibodies, particularly IgA, are important mechanisms of protection against GI tract

infections. While these mucosal adaptive immune responses can be elicited by natural infections

or mucosal vaccines, they are poorly induced by vaccination via parenteral routes, such as by

subcutaneous (s.c.) or intramuscular (i.m.) injections (Figure 1.2). Lack of local protection results

in less effective blocking of pathogen entry, shredding and transmission, as is the case for the

inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) (Hird & Grassly, 2012).


<!-- Page 18 -->


8

Despite their low GI protection, s.c. and i.m. vaccines hold strengths in systemic

immunogenicity, effectiveness of adjuvants, and diversity of delivery platforms such as mRNA

and subunit vaccines. Many vaccines against GI tract diseases, clinically or in development, are

administered through s.c. or i.m. routes.

*Figure 1.2 Graphic Illustration*

Vaccines delivered parenterally (through the skin) do not provide lymphocytes with the properties

needed (“gut-imprinting”) to access the intestinal mucosa.

Strategies that target T cells and IgA responses to the gut upon parenteral vaccination can

enhance protection against GI infections, while circumventing the many challenges of oral vaccine

development. One such targeting approach is the supplementation of parenteral vaccines with

tissue-specific signals that directs trafficking of antigen-experienced lymphocytes to the small

intestine.

### 1.4 REGULATION OF INTESTINAL TRAFFICKING BY RETIONIC ACID

### 1.4.1 Trafficking of T cells to Non-lymphoid Tissues

While naïve T cells circulate through the blood, the lymph and secondary lymphoid organs,

antigen-experienced T cells can migrate to sites where the antigen is seen and carry out their

immune functions.

The trafficking of T cells to peripheral tissues, or “T cell homing”, is a multistep process

dependent on specific adhesion receptors and chemokine receptors on the T cell surface (von

Andrian & Mackay, 2000). These receptors interact with their ligands on endothelial cells in the

post-capillary venules of specific tissues, mediating T cell adhesion to and migration across the

vascular wall in a step-wise manner.

Unique combinations of primary adhesion, chemokine and secondary adhesion receptors

mediate T cell homing to specific peripheral tissues. These receptors are proposed to be regulated

by the environment of the secondary lymphoid organs during antigen stimulation. For the skin

(Mora et al., 2005), the small intestine (Mora et al., 2003) and colon (Dzutsev et al., 2017),

dendritic cells (DCs) have been identified as the major regulators.

### 1.4.2 T cell Trafficking to the Small Intestine

Teff homing to non-inflamed small intestine (SI) mucosa is mediated by α4ꞵ7 integrin

(Berlin et al., 1993) and CCR9 (Zabel et al., 1999), respectively interacting with MAdCAM-1 and

CCL25 on endothelial cells. All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), a metabolite of vitamin A that is

abundant in the SI, is shown to mediate the “imprinting” of the SI homing property on Teff cells

(Eksteen et al., 2009; Iwata et al., 2004a; Svensson et al., 2008). In mLN and PP, CD103+ DCs are

proposed as the major source of ATRA (Coombes et al., 2007)(Fig 1.3). In line with this, co-culture


<!-- Page 20 -->


10

with PP and mLN DCs up-regulates α4β7 and CCR9 on Teff and directs them to the SI (Mora et

al., 2003).

*Figure 1.3 Retinoic acid induces T cell homing to SI (Bono et al., 2016)*

Whether ATRA indirectly regulates T cell homing through DCs has not been shown. It is

hypothesized that ATRA directly regulates transcription of α4β7 and CCR9 in Teff upon antigen-

activation, through a RARα-RXR heterodimer which binds to RARE sequences in the regulative

regions of the genes encoding α4 integrin and CCR9 (Kang et al., 2011; Ohoka et al., 2011), and

increases their transcription when ATRA is present. The up-regulation of CCR9 by ATRA requires

cooperativity with TCR signaling. ATRA doesn’t increase β7 expression in vitro, and the increase

in α4β7 is thought to be due to increased availability of α4 to dimerize with the β7 subunit (Denucci

et al., n.d.; Kang et al., 2011)


<!-- Page 21 -->


11

The effects of ATRA on each T cell subset under inflamed and homeostatic conditions are

not fully characterized. Moreover, in vitro studies on how ATRA regulates T cells might not fully

recapitulate in vivo conditions, since additional regulative factors might be missing. In accordance

with this, discrepancies exist between in vitro and in vivo data for T cell homing properties and

immune functions upon exposure to ATRA (Bono et al., 2016).

### 1.5 REGULATION OF LARGE INTESTINE TRAFFICKING BY THE ARYL-

HYDROCARBON RECEPTOR

### 1.5.1 Overview of AHR

The aryl-hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) is another key transcription regulator of gut

immunity. AHR is a member of the PAS [periodic circadian protein (PER)–AHR nuclear

translocator (ARNT)–single-minded protein (SIM)] superfamily of transcription factors (Gu et al.,

2000). While best known functionally for sensing of xenobiotic compounds and removal of toxins,

AHR also plays important roles in tissue homeostasis and immune regulation.

In the inactive state, AHR is kept in the cytosol within a protein complex consisting of heat

shock protein (Hsp90), prostaglandin E synthase 3 (p23), proto-oncogene non-receptor tyrosine

kinase (SRC), and the AHR-interacting protein (AIP). Agonist binding to AHR induces the

translocation into the nucleus, binding to AHR nuclear translocator (ARNT), binding to AHR-

responsive DNA elements, and subsequent transcription regulation of the target gene

(Rothhammer & Quintana, 2019).(Figure 1.4)

*Figure 1.4 Signaling and transcription regulation of AHR (Rothhammer & Quintana, 2019)*

Many compounds can act as ligands for AHR, including xenobiotic compounds

(environmental toxins) such as TCDD, and physiological ligands from diet and microbiota sources.

Of interest, tryptophan metabolites are a key class of AHR ligands, which is produced in the

intestinal tract by both host and microbiota metabolism.

### 1.5.2 Regulation of Large Intestine Trafficking by AHR

While it has been long known that AHR is an important regulator of intestinal immunity,

particularly in the differentiation of regulatory T cells (Treg) (Quintana et al., 2008), the role of

AHR in promoting colon trafficking is only recently described.

GPR15, a G-protein coupled receptor, has been identified as a key molecule in mediating

regulatory T cell (Treg) trafficking to the large intestine (Kim et al., 2013).  Later studies

demonstrated that in CD4+ T cells, expression of GPR15 is regulated by AHR (Swaminathan et

al., 2021), and that the AHR-Foxp3-RORγt axis controls CD4+ T cell gut homing by regulating

GPR15 (Xiong et al., 2020a). Additionally, AHR has also been proposed to enhance the

establishment of resident memory T cells (Dean et al., 2023). However, the role of AHR in

regulating GPR15 in CD8+ T cells, and in regulating CD8+ T cell trafficking to the intestine

remains to be studied.

### 2.1 INTRODUCTION

All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) is a metabolite of dietary vitamin A that is abundant in the

GI tract. Upon oral antigen encounter, T cells and B cells are activated in the mesenteric lymph

nodes (mLNs) and Peyer’s Patches (PPs), where ATRA activates their retinoic acid receptor (RAR)

to up-regulate gut-homing molecules α4ꞵ7 and CCR9 (“tissue-imprinting”)(Iwata et al., 2004b).

α4ꞵ7 and CCR9 respectively interact with MadCAM1 and CCL25 on post-capillary venular

endothelial cells of the small intestine and mediate trafficking of antigen-experienced lymphocytes

into the small intestine mucosa. Apart from directing gut-trafficking, it was showed in a recent

study (Qiu et al., 2023) that retinoic acid signaling plays a role in promoting the in situ

differentiation of tissue-resident memory T cells in the gut, which may provide additional benefits

in vaccine response.

Taking advantage of this physiological mechanism, Hammerschmidt et al described the

used of parenteral ATRA in generating gut-tropic vaccine responses (Hammerschmidt et al., 2011).

In this study, multiple high doses of ATRA were injected over the span of 2 weeks, which elicited

T cell and IgA responses in the small intestine and improved protection against Salmonella

challenge.

This dosing regimen, while effective, presents challenges for clinical translation due to the

need for frequent injections. Nano-carrier technologies enable more efficient and sustained

delivery of ATRA and are attractive strategies for reducing the dose and injection frequency,

thereby improving the clinical translatability of using ATRA for gut-targeting. A few encapsulation

strategies have been reported (Christensen et al., 2019; Du et al., 2019).

I characterized the gut-targeting efficacy of Am80, a synthetic RAR agonist, and studied

the establishment of memory compartments following vaccination. Am80 is more stable than

ATRA and is clinically tested for acute promyelocytic leukemia treatment (Miwako & Kagechika,

2007; Shinagawa et al., 2012; Tobita et al., 1997). Its effectiveness in mediating gut-trafficking

upon s.c. vaccination has not been characterized.

Supplementing a parenteral subunit vaccine with gut-imprinting compound Am80

successfully targeted CD8+ T cells to the small intestine (SI). Upon this validation of imprinting

efficacy, I report the identification and validation of a novel Am80-encapsulating acetylated-

dextran based polymeric nanoparticle (Ac-Dex-NP) which achieved effective SI targeting with a

single injection, thus lowering the cumulative Am80 dose and enhancing clinical translatability. In

summary, adjuvantation with RAR ligands is a viable strategy for enhancing GI tract vaccine

responses of parenteral vaccines.

### 2.2.3 Am80 was effectively encapsulated in an acetylated-dextran based nano-carrier

Since proof-of-principle studies with unformulated Am80 demonstrated small intestine

### 2.3 METHODS

Animal Study

Adult C57BL/6 mice were obtained from Jackson Laboratories. OT-1 β-actin GFP mice

were bred by crossing β-actin GFP and OT-1 strains, obtained from Jackson Laboratories. Mice

were housed and procedures were performed at Harvard Medical School animal facility. Animal

protocols were reviewed and approved by the Harvard IACUC.

Materials and Reagents

See Supplemental Materials

OT-1 in vitro Culture

Splenocytes of OT-1 mice were plated at 150k OT-1 cells per well in 96-well round-bottom

plates, in 200ul complete T cell media and treated with 10nM of Am80 or nanoparticles, in the

presence of 100ug/ml (20ug per well) OVA for 3 days. At 66-72 hours, cells were harvested,

stained with antibodies, and analyzed by flow cytometry.

OT-1 in vivo Assay (Parenteral Immunization)

Mice were adoptively transferred with OT-1 cells, and subsequently immunized with

100µg chicken ovalbumin (OVA) and an adjuvant CpG-1668 (0.5 nmol). On day 0,1 and 2, mice

were injected s.c. with solvent control (DMSO or ethanol/ETOH in PEG-400), retinoic acid

receptor agonist Am80 (500 nmol in PEG-400), or nano-carriers w/wo Am80 encapsulation. At

timepoints defined by individual experiments, tissues were harvested and analyzed.


<!-- Page 40 -->


30

Preparing intestinal samples for flow cytometry

Small intestine (duodenum to ileum) was dissected out and flushed. Peyer’s patches and

fat were removed, and the tissue was cut into 4-5 pieces, and flipped to expose the luminal surface.

Tissue pieces were washed for 30min at 37C in HBSS+2.5%FBS+2.5mM EDTA and IEL fraction

was collected by passing through metal mesh strainer. Tissue was further minced into small pieces

and digested for 30min at 37C in HBSS+2.5% FBS, with Collagenase D and DNase1. LPL fraction

was collected by filtering through mesh strainer. Both IEL and LPL fractions were further

subjected to a 36%-67% percoll gradient. The interphase is collected and resuspended in FACS

buffer (PBS+2%BSA+2mM EDTA), stained for 30min on ice with antibodies and Fc block,

washed and resuspended for flow cytometry analysis.

Cell Count and Flow Cytometry

For cell counting, samples were diluted and counted on a BD Accuri C6 Plus cytometer.

For flow cytometry, samples were run on a Beckman CytoFLEX cytometer, and analysis was done

using Flow Jo software V10.

IDISCO clearing and Confocal Microscopy

A 1-2cm piece of the small intestine was harvested, cut open longitudinally, and fixed flat

with 4% PFA in a cassette, at 4C overnight. Tissue was then subjected to IDISCO clearing protocol

as previously described (Renier et al., 2014). Images were acquired on point-scanning confocal

microscope (Olympus FV3000), and multiple fields of view were taken per sample. Analysis was

done on Imaris software with function for dot counting and surface area calculation.

Preparation of Serum and Fecal Samples for ELISA

For serum, blood was collected through submandibular vein (cheek bleed), coagulated for

30 min at 37 C and centrifuged at 500g for 5 min. The serum (supernatant) was taken and stored

at -20C. For fecal samples, fecal pellets were reconstituted at 50-200mg/ml in PBS containing

cOmplete protease inhibitor, by vigorous vertexing or beating with bead raptor for 2min at 4m/s.

Pathology

### 2.4 DISCUSSIONS

In summary, I characterized small intestine targeting of CD8+ T cells and IgA antibodies

upon parenteral administration of Am80, a synthetic RAR agonist, and validated a novel Am80-

encapsulating polymeric nanoparticle with improved delivery and clinical translatability.

Local inflammatory stimuli and antigen re-encounter have been implicated in the

augmentation of CD8+ T cells and formation of resident memory in peripheral tissues. Due to the

complexity of the gut environment in which many studies were conducted, it was at times difficult

to tease apart the effects of specific treatments on trafficking, retention, and memory formation.

The parenteral vaccination approach offers a model to drive CD8+ T cells to the homeostatic tissue,

therefore allowing the study of tissue trafficking and memory formation processes, disentangled

from the effects of local inflammation and immune challenge.

Along these lines, while a role for low-grade inflammation, from micro-abrasions, food

antigens and microbiota cannot be ruled out, our data suggested the ability to establish Trm cells in

non-challenged small intestine, characterized by expression of CD103 and CD69. Notably, Qiu et

al published recent study on the role of retinoic acid in licensing Trm differentiation in the gut (Qiu

et al., 2023). It would be of interest, in future studies, to compare Trm cells formed in the

homeostatic versus immune-challenged gut environment, to further tease apart how local tissue

environments affect the formation, phenotype and longevity of resident memory T cells.

Trial and errors in encapsulating AM80 suggested some desirable features in dosing, LN

profiles and others for successfully formulating gut-targeting compounds for s.c. administration.

In accordance with other studies (Stary et al., 2015), the data suggested a key window for the

tissue-imprinting of antigen-experienced CD8+ T cells. In the parenteral vaccination approach,

access to sufficient levels of imprinting signals, throughout the first 48-72 hours following antigen


<!-- Page 43 -->


33

encounter, was essential for the robust induction of gut-tropism.  Therefore, strategies aimed at

utilizing imprinting compounds need to ensure these compounds are accessible at sufficient

amounts at the initiating secondary lymphoid organ within this period.

I identify several limitations of the study.

First, OVA is used as a model antigen for the study due to the plentifulness and robustness

of tools for tracking antigen-specific immune responses. However, it is not a relevant antigen for

a real-world vaccine. While it could be speculated that the mechanisms governing lymphocyte

trafficking will also be applicable to other localized antigen + adjuvant combinations, this remains

to be demonstrated.

Second, mice studies might not recapitulate human biology, therefore the clinical

feasibility of the parenteral approach remains to be proved.

Third, a method for scaling up production of Ac-Dex-NP is needed for translational

purposes, and the full pre-clinical evaluation of toxicity, pharmacokinetics and other drug

properties remains to be carried out. Additionally, RAR signaling is involved in many other

pathways, and the effects of Ac-Dex-NP on other cells and biological processes need to be

considered.

### 3.1 INTRODUCTION

Having shown that RAR signaling targets CD8+ T cells responses to the small intestine, I

next asked how CD8+ T cells can be directed to the large intestine. Many enteric pathogens, such

as Polio, invade and/or colonize both the small intestine and the large intestine. Therefore, targeting

immunity to the small intestine, while beneficial, might not be sufficient to fully protect against

infection. Given this challenge, I asked if a parental vaccine model could be achieved that confers

total intestinal tract protection.

The signals and pathways that target CD8+ T cells to the large intestine have not been fully

understood. However, recent studies have indicated that the aryl-hydrocarbon receptor (AHR)

plays an important role in CD4+ T cell, particularly Treg cell trafficking to the large intestine

through up-regulation of GPR15 (Kim et al., 2013; Swaminathan et al., 2021; Xiong et al., 2020a).

These findings raised the questions whether GPR15 also mediates large intestine trafficking in

CD8+ T cells, and whether CD8+ T cells up-regulated GPR15 upon activation of AHR signaling.

Moreover, since α4ꞵ7 is known to mediate large intestine trafficking, I asked how RAR signaling

and AHR signaling interact to regulate trafficking to the small and large intestine.

In this chapter, I showed that combined targeting of RAR and AHR generated a large

intestine-tropic CD8+ T cell population, enhanced lymphocyte trafficking to the cecum, colon and

rectum, promoted establishment of tissue resident memory, and improved protection of the

colorectal mucosa against infection.

Animal Study

Adult C57BL/6 mice and BALB/c mice were obtained from Jackson Laboratories. OT-1

### 3.4 DISCUSSION

In summary, I identified and validated a parenteral vaccination strategy for optimal

targeting of CD8+ T effector cells to small and large intestine through targeting of the RAR and

AHR signaling pathways.

I showed that activation of AHR in CD8+ T effector cells increased expression of GPR15

in vitro and in vivo, with a possible requirement for TGFβ1. Combined treatment with RAR and

AHR agonists generated a population of α4ꞵ7+GPR15+ Teff cells that were optimized for

trafficking to the large intestine. Deficiency in either the RAR-α4ꞵ7 or AHR-GPR15 pathways

reduced trafficking to the large intestine, while trafficking to the small intestine was not affected

by AHR signaling. These findings suggested differential requirements for lymphocytes trafficking

to separate intestinal segments.

The combined targeting method increased the establishment of tissue-resident memory T

cells in the small and large intestinal mucosa in the absence of local inflammation and immune

challenge. Furthermore, this method could be utilized as a vaccination approach to boost vaccine

protection against gut pathogens, especially those whose invasion and colonization engages the

entire length of the intestinal tract. Potentially, protection of the large intestine could also be

considered in the context of sexually transmitted diseases and colorectal cancer.

I identified several limitations of this study.

(1)  The effects of AHR on other cell types and biological processes remain to be

characterized. AHR is a key transcription regulator with many diverse functions in various cell

types. While our data strongly suggested a T cell intrinsic trafficking phenotype, it is plausible that

AHR also affected many other aspects of the vaccine response, leading to increased gut trafficking,

tissue residency, and protection.


<!-- Page 78 -->


68

(2) The effects of other AHR ligands on up-regulation of GPR15 have not been

characterized. AHR can be activated by many diverse families of compounds, and there have been

reports of different ligands leading to different downstream signaling. It is plausible that only

certain groups of AHR ligands could promote GPR15 expression.

(3) Animal studies do not fully reflect human biology, and whether this strategy is

applicable clinically in humans requires further investigation.

Additionally, the study was carried out using parenteral supplementation of synthetic AHR

and RAR agonists. Whether this reflects the physiology, and what constitutes endogenous

bioactive AHR ligand in the large intestine environment, remains to be understood. An attractive

hypothesis is that AHR ligands derived by host or microbiota provide tissue-imprinting signal, but

this remains to be demonstrated.

Summary of Proposed Model

In summary, I showed that CD8+ T cell trafficking to the small and large intestine are

differentially regulated. While trafficking to the small intestine only requires RAR signaling,

trafficking to the large intestine requires a combination of RAR and AHR signaling. Adjuvantation

of parenteral vaccines with agonists of RAR and AHR, either un-encapsulated or in nano-carrier

formulations, are viable approaches to enhance T cell protection of GI tract (Figure 4.1). The major

findings of this study offer new insights into how T cell responses are within distinct segments of

the intestinal tract, and further augments our understanding of how tissue environment interacts

with the entry of lymphocytes into peripheral tissue.

Regulation of GPR15 expression

The full requirements for CD8+ T cell expression of GPR15 has not been mapped out, and

there were several differences between in vitro and in vivo results.

Notably, supplementation of TGFβ1 and IL-2 are critical to GPR15 expression in vitro, but

not in the in vivo vaccination setting. It could be argued that the lymph node milieu provided access

to TGFβ1 and IL-2, as well as other cytokine signals that remain to be identified. Given the

involvement of TGFβ1, it could be asked whether GPR15 expression is regulated on the intestinal

mucosa, in addition to in the draining lymph node. Additionally, it is unclear whether DC-T cell

interactions are needed for the expression of GPR15.

Our data suggested that ATRA and Am80 had a significant inhibitory effect on the

expression of GPR15, particularly in vitro but also in vivo to a lesser extent. Particularly, in our in

vitro study, the addition of ATRA concurrently with 10-CL-BBQ, but not 24 hours or 48 hours

after, fully abrogated GPR15 expression. The mechanism for this inhibition is not understood and

would need to be elucidated using molecular and biochemical techniques.  Several hypotheses

could be made, such as (1) inhibition of AHR nuclear translocation and signaling; (2) inhibition of

GPR15 protein synthesis and stability; (3) shared signaling molecules between RAR and AHR

pathways leading to competition of resources.

Additionally, knockout of AHR did not fully abrogate the expression of GPR15, both in

my study and in published research (Xiong et al., 2020b). This suggests additional mechanisms

that regulate GPR15 expression, possibly involving TGF β1 signaling, which remain to be

understood.


<!-- Page 82 -->


72

Physiological Role of the AHR-GPR15 Axis

While supplementing a parenteral vaccine with gut-imprinting compounds allowed us to

study T cell trafficking without confounding factors in the gut environment, the conclusions we

obtained might not fully recapitulate gut physiology.

Particularly, future studies are needed to uncover whether the AHR-GPR15 axis indeed

dictates large intestine trafficking for CD8+ T cells. To this end, oral antigen challenge and

infection models could be used, and expression of GPR15, as well as gut trafficking of

AHR/GPR15 deficient cells could be analyzed.

Segmented immune responses in the intestinal tract has been proposed by several studies

(Esterházy et al., 2019b; Houston et al., 2016b; Veenbergen et al., 2017b), and our study provides

another line of evidence for the differential regulation of T cell responses between the small and

large intestine. It has not yet been demonstrated whether trafficking to the small or large intestine

is dictated by the environment of the draining lymph node where a cell is primed. Additionally,

since RAR signaling suppressed GPR15 expression in our study, it raised the question of whether

and how this inhibition is regulated in vivo, so that cells could be differentially destined to either

the small intestine or the large intestine.

Moreover, it is not known yet what specific gut metabolites are serving as the physiological

AHR ligand for this tissue-imprinting process. It could be argued that an “imprinting” signal would

be unique to and abundant in the large intestine, which makes microbial metabolites attractive

targets for future studies. A large array of dietary and microbial compounds has been identified as

AHR ligands, and a method to effectively screen these compounds would be crucial to addressing

this question.


<!-- Page 83 -->

Implications for Vaccine Development

While we obtained preliminary evidence that enhanced protection was generated by our

vaccination strategy (Am80+10-CL-BBQ), it should be noted that there are caveats to the

challenge model. The human disease pathogenesis for many enteric pathogens is not well

replicated by animal studies, and we have been limited to enteric pathogens that could be studied

using a mouse model. In our setting, high doses of Listeria needed to be used, which was super-

physiological and could confound our readout. Additionally, we have yet to show that Am80+10-

CL-BBQ generated Trm cells were the cause of the enhanced protection, as opposed to other effects

of Am80+10-CL-BBQ on the animal.

It would be of interest to test the effects of Am80+10-CL-BBQ in combination with real-

world vaccines as well as different vaccine modalities (such as mRNA vaccine), in animal models

with either good mimicry of human disease, or with well-characterized immune correlates of

protection. While this adjuvantation strategy could, in theory, be combined with any antigen +

adjuvant, it would likely be most cost-effective for infections where T cells play an important role

in pathogen clearance (norovirus, poliovirus, rotavirus, HIV, Listeria, Salmonella, etc), and for

infections with a high global disease burden.

Mucosal antigen-specific IgA is another key mechanism for protection against infections.

While we are limited in scope to fully characterize intestinal IgA responses in our vaccination

settings, preliminary data (not shown) suggested a boost in intestinal IgA responses as well in

Am80+10-CL-BBQ treated animals, in addition to CD8+ T cell responses. This needs to be further

studied and could be an additional layer of enhanced vaccine protection, particularly against

pathogen entry, and against extracellular bacteria.


<!-- Page 84 -->


74

Additionally, our targeting strategy could potentially be utilized in other disease settings

where presence of CD8+ T cells could be beneficial. It would be of interest to test whether

adjuvantation of AM80+10-CL-BBQ could improve efficacy of therapeutic vaccines for colorectal

cancer, and whether in vitro generated intestinal-tropic cells could be used in adoptive cell

therapies, such as for colorectal cancer and for inflammatory bowel disease (using cultured Treg

cells).

Lastly, while 10-CL-BBQ was used for my study, it is very plausible that other ligands,

synthetic or physiological, would have more favorable characteristics for clinical use. Screening

and pharmacological assessments would be needed to identify the most promising compounds for

clinical translation. As many AHR ligands are poorly soluble in aqueous solutions, encapsulation

strategies, such as the one presented in Chapter Two for Am80, could potentially be explored for

more effective delivery of AHR ligand, and co-delivery of Am80 + AHR ligand.
